links.reason: Verse 279 likens an earthly realm to the sky-world ('வானுல கொப்பது'); it does not praise heaven itself, so it is not the heaven Naladiyar 137 weighs against learned company. Only the word heaven joins them.

Naladiyar-style prudential advice against travel (தேசாந்திரங்களும் செல்லாதே) and a hero's leaving are different advice for different situations; line 1-2 of 1176 is itself uncertain, and the epic's road (elephants, ghoul-women) is not the Siddhar's list (tiger, courtesan).
links.text_issue: Lines 1-3 of 1176 are obscure (விடுத்தன் மேயினார்; கூற்று/காற்றின); the fish-in-a-well reading is the marker's.

links.reason: Udayanan wards off arrows and shoots back (எய்தான்), while the Kural's elephant only stands (ஊன்றுங் களிறு). The verse names no steadiness, so the epic does not extend the couplet, it merely shows a brave man under arrows.

1148 is a boast of overturning mountains and rolling the world; nothing in it is rage, and TM 1686 lists பெருமை கூறலும் among a long set whose sense (of the Lord or of those near Him) the marker admits is uncertain. 'Great-hearted rage' is not in the Tamil.

The hero says wealth is the keenest steel (Kural 759), and the poem's hero at 11-15 thinks of the girl who asked 'நீட்டுவிர் அல்லிரோ' as he leaves for wealth hard to earn (ஈட்டு அருங் குரைய பொருள்). The pair adds a cost the bare imperative leaves out. 'Always' in teaches is a little strong.

1445 is Asvagriva's boast; 1448 answers 'குன்றின்மேல் இருந்து நீ நின் குழுவினுள் மொழிவ தல்லால் இன்று வந்து என் முன் நின்றும்' - the reply directly reverses the boast's setting. A real answer within one scene.

Kural 61 ranks wise children the greatest gain; 1760 lists wealth, victory, friends, wives and children as things that can be got (நண்ணலாகும்) but says a brother cannot be made (ஆக்கலாகா). That sets a limit on the Kural's list from outside it.

1784 shows the widow worshipping with unanointed hair (பூசுதலும் இன்றி); the greens and gravel bed of the Puram poem are not in this verse, and the epic nowhere weighs pyre against widowhood. The claimed opposite valuation rests on verses outside the packet.

2776 sends killers to hell (செல்ப நரகந் தன்னுள் தீவினைத் தேர்கள் ஊர்ந்தே) and Kural 321 says killing brings all other deeds (பிறவினை எல்லாந் தரும்). Real but illustration; the verse does not name killing the root of other sins and also sends deniers of the next world there.
262 shows Vegavati taking Madanamanjikai's shape, which carries out the guile (சூது) of 261. That is plot sequence with a modest fulfilment; 'search turned into the means' is not in the Tamil.

803 shows Civakan laughing as a ghoul dresses in the dead (நக்கான்); patikam 28 says household and hero renounce. These are not incompatible claims, and 'relishing slaughter' is not what the verse says; it is sequence in a life.

2951 has wives asking 'நீத்தியோ' whether he will cast them off; 1097 is Civakan, bound and led away, forbidding grief. The wives are not quoting him and 'asking for what he refused' is not in either text; the shared theme is attachment.

The note rests on the number three and ஒன்றி, which may go with 'sent'. Nothing says the spies were ignorant of one another or gave one report ('இன்று இதால் பட்டது'), so the Kural's safeguard is not tested.

1967 says those who take great austerity then practise deceit (மாதவம் ஏற்றுக் கொண்டு மாயங்கள் பின்னை முயல்வார்) are born as beasts; the Kural's hunter in the bush is not in the verse and the 'hunted' reversal is not stated. A rebirth consequence added to a condemned fault, not the same image.

Both give the three-forts deed with a mountain bow, serpent string and a single arrow (நாகம் நாணா மலை வில்லாக ... ஓர் அழல்-அம்பின் / பாம்புஞாண் கொளீஇ ஒரு கணை) and the forehead eye. Common formula used for counsel in one and prelude to birth in the other.
484 turns on மாமான், unclear; 489 does say the water is for Padumukan (பதுமுக குமரற்கு என்றே). The fulfilment is real, but 'his own rule of rank' is not in either verse.

1576 has lovers' eyes covered by the beloved as senses fail; TM 152 has the body-house dismantled, nine gates shut, kin weeping. Same theme of death, but the epic does not develop TM, and the 'loving ones' are not identified with the bed-women in either text.
141 gives the just king's catalogue (ஐய கோல், ஏக ஆணை); 198 shows him 'மண் அகம் காவலின் வழுக்கி' for his queen. The later verse reverses the portrait of the earlier.

The speaker of 71 says he won the prince's ornaments by dice (சூதினால் செயித்து நின் சுதன் அணிகள் கொண்டனன்) and then the prince beat him twice; it is not the prince winning from kings and giving back. The 'winner who gives back' of teaches is not in the Tamil.

1 says the god reached bliss தன்னின் (by/from himself); 29 says Civakan attained a flood of bliss. The 'walking the same road' framing is the marker's reading, and the 29 simile (nectar, no longer wanting women) says nothing of effort.

Both turn the battle into a farm: sowing arrows/spears (வித்தி), corpse crop, ghouls fed (பேய்க்கூழ் / பேய்மகள்). The shared image is real; 'develops' asserts a derivation the Tamil does not show, and the speaker of 757 is inferred.
links.text_issue: Speaker of 757 inferred; sense flagged uncertain.

links.reason: Both put a king's fault and the world's suffering (அறந்தலை மயங்கி வையம் பட; முறைகோடி ... பெயல்) but 263 is a simile of the sun scorching the sea; 'heat not drought' is the vehicle, not a claim the epic makes beyond the Kural.

626 has the learned man earn, draw in, guard and give wealth (காத்து உயர் ஈகை) and become protector of others, which maps on Kural 385's ஈட்டல், காத்தல், வகுத்தல்; it adds the condition of learning (கற்றவன்).

2127 praises the liberated hero (கேவலப் பேரொளி), 1 praises the Arhat who conquered karma; the two are different persons and no 'war' is won in 2127 (Death and Desire leave). The title echo is real, the ring-composition claim overstated.

Both are Jain praise of the Jina with flowers (மலர்) and refuge; 1467 states non-praisers miss release (வீட்டுலகம் நண்ணாரே), 1609 asks how not to praise (பழிச்சாவா றென்னே). Neither limits the other, so qualifies is wrong.
454 shows the herd recovered by bow-sound (சிலையின் ஒலியால்); patikam 11 summarises the same deed. The note about வள்ளல் anticipating a bloodless manner stretches the epithet.

101 lists wall engines (பொறி) and defences; it does not say the wall lacks defenders and the next verse continues the list. The Kural's 'wall without active men' is imposed as a criticism the epic does not make.
links.text_issue: Catalogue continues into 102; no finite verb.

links.reason: 1861 is a vow with a curse on fame (என் பெயர் சேறல் இன்றாய்), 72 a vanjinam with poets ceasing to sing (புலவர் பாடாது வரைக). The form matches but 'develops' claims descent; the 'raiders prove friends' and 'plot empties' in teaches come from outside this verse.

Kural 1130: the town says he is loveless (ஏதிலர் என்னும் இவ் ஊர்); Kuruntokai 289 line 8: the town pities her more than she pities him (நம்மினும் நம் திறத்து இரங்கும் ஊர்). That limits the stock hostile ur.

2130 shows two princes worshipping under the lord's feet; 2 says the poet will tell the story of one who went to him for refuge. The identification of the princes is by colour alone, and refuge to worship is a thin arc.
links.text_issue: Princes identified by colour only; Soolamani 2 line 1 may be misprinted.

links.reason: Both pit a lamp against darkness: 2018 வினை எனும் தீ இருள, the lamp being காட்சி; Naladiyar 51 lamp of தவம் and darkness returns when oil fails. The source of the light and the limit differ, which each lacks.

190 names Vasavadatta as the measure (வாசவதத்தை தன் வண்கையினது அதனைப் போல); 103 only has her brought to learn, with who teaches uncertain. A callback, but the 'tie began here' claim is outside the Tamil.

72 has sulking women say 'கண் உளார் நும் காதலர்'; Kural 1311 charges that all women feast on him with their eyes. The accusations differ (rivals in his eyes versus others looking at him), so qualifies is unsupported; the eye motif is shared.

Naga 165 says release comes by meditation on the self (உயிர் தியானம்); TM 219 says fire worship burns deeds. The epic does not exclude a fire rite and TM names no rival means, so no dispute over 'who burns' is in the texts.

119 has worshippers of the lotus-seated lord's feet become Indras; Kural 3 has those who reach the feet of one who walked on the flower live long. The lotus is stock and the tirthankara is not named, so 'Jain case of the flower-borne god' is imposed.

1907 argues trees live from their flowering at a woman's look and mocks deniers; Neelakesi 367 argues from seasonal change that trees have life. Same Jain thesis in two registers, with different evidence.

Both have evening coming 'like killers' (கொல்லுநர் போல வரும் / கொலைக்களத்து ஏதிலர் போல வரும்); the shared simile is real but priority and 'develops' are not shown, and Kural 1224 does not say it is one woman's private complaint.

934 shows the king under the umbrella and says he guards all evenly; Kural 389 conditions the world's shelter on tolerance. The epic does not limit or contradict, and 'display cannot show character' is the grader's gloss.
302 shows Vijayai weeping alone for her lord; 2138 has her end the palace's lament (விலாவணை நீக்கினாள்). A reversal in her role, not incompatible claims, and 'counsel of revenge' is not in the verse.

1963 states restraint (நிறை) and desire cannot dwell together; 1964 shows desire seizing her (தலைக்கொண்டது காம வெந்தீ) after she steadied herself. That fits her claim as much as it refutes it, since restraint gives way.

2072 shows the father (நாய்கன்) unable to accept or refuse; 907 is his purchase of the royal order. The earlier act is a cause, but the Tamil gives his bind to their lack of penance (நோற்றிலாதேன்), not to the order.

250 says counsel is the highest of the king's three powers; 237 is the same king (marker's speaker for both) saying life lacks flower without counsel. A repeat of one thesis, and teaches calls 237 the poet's maxim.

269 has Saccandan say birth and death come from deeds' fruit and sorrow from lack of fine understanding; Naladiyar 110 says the early mark is fixed so grief is useless. The 'confession' reading depends on 260-261, not on this verse. The fate-versus-deed contrast is real.

1611 gives Kama-scorching to the Jina (காமனையுங் காய்ந்த); TM 346 speaks of the yoga that destroys Kama's work at Korukkai, a verse whose sense is uncertain and that does not claim the burning for Siva. Two claims on one feat are not shown incompatible.
